newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia edges closer to final Chechnya pullout.
newsitem.headline: Russia edges closer to final Chechnya pullout.

text.p: Russia said on Sunday it had pulled its last Interior Ministry troops from Chechnya, edging a step closer towards a formal end of the bloody, two-year conflict in the breakaway region.

The withdrawal, ordered by President Boris Yeltsin to pave the way for elections in Chechnya on January 27, was announced by the troops' chief of staff Lieutenant-General Pavel Maslov, who said it had gone smoothly and according to plan.

A spokesman for the Defence Ministry said an unknown number of army troops were still in the region, where they were sent by Yeltsin to crush separatist moves in December 1994. He could not say exactly when they would be withdrawn.
Confusion has surrounded the timetable for the troop withdrawal, ordered by Yeltsin in November to meet the demands of separatists who signed a peace deal with Moscow in August.
RIA news agency quoted Maslov as saying conflicting reports had been intentional and dictated by the need "to avoid possible provocations".

The separatists, who repeatedly humiliated the Russian military during 21 months of fighting which killed tens of thousands of people, agreed to postpone a decision on Chechnya's status in return for the troop withdrawal.
But they have stuck firmly to independence declarations during the run-up to the election for a regional leader and parliament which will replace the administration installed by Moscow.

A ceasefire has held in Chechnya since the August peace deal but sporadic violence has continued and Tim Guldimann, the Swiss diplomat trying to help broker a permanent peace deal, said that he was concerned for the safety of foreign election observers.
Six foreign Red Cross workers were shot dead in their beds in a hospital compound in Chechnya last month and Guldimann said this had exacerbated the safety problem.
"The Russian federal authorities are prepared to extend comprehensive coooperation to the international observers and promised to grant them visas without delay," RIA quoted Guldimann as saying.

"Nevertheless, much will depend on whether the Chechen authorities can supply tangible guarantees of the observers' safety," added the diplomat, who heads a mission in Chechnya of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

The separatists are keen to have foreign observers present during voting to add legitimacy to the elections, which they see as a first step towards an independence recognised beyond Chechen frontiers.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky has said Moscow -- which insists Chechnya must remain part of Russia -- does not object to their presence but that it is up to the separatists who are now running the region to ensure their safety.
Guldimann said a final decision on the observers would be made at a meeting of the Council of Europe in Vienna on January 16 at which he would report on the situation in Chechnya.
The five main candidates for the presidency -- all members of the separatist leadership -- were due to meet later on Sunday to see if they could unite around a single candidate.

But RIA quoted sources close to separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, who initiated the meeting, as saying they saw little hope of success due to tensions between Yandarbiyev and former rebel chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov, the poll favourite.
